brief.protagonist: PRP Real Assets, a D.C.-based investment firm that just bought 900 19th St. NW, a 117K SF office building that is roughly 60% vacant.
brief.stakes: PRP paid around $30M for a building with three empty floors and plans to invest six figures into improvements to attract an anchor tenant. If they succeed, they create value from a distressed asset; if not, they own a mostly empty building in a soft office market.
brief.tension: The building is 60% vacant, yet PRP bought it and will put more money in. The tension is between the current owner's unwillingness to reinvest and PRP's bet that a 'good building, bad balance sheet' can be turned around. There is no explicit clock, but the vacancy and need for lease-up create urgency.
brief.why_now: The deal closed on Tuesday, and it is an example of a 'basis reset' in D.C. office, where investors are buying distressed assets at low prices to reposition them.
brief.number_that_matters: 60% vacancy: that means three empty floors, each 16K SF, which could be an anchor tenant opportunity but also means the building is mostly empty. Paid around $30M for 117K SF, roughly $256/SF, a steep discount from prior values.
brief.lens_note: PRP is buying at a 'basis reset' after Tishman Speyer owned it since 2006 and completed a substantial renovation in 2017. Tishman is selling a vacant building while dealing with distress at nearby International Square. PRP sees an opportunity to reinvest where the current owner may not be interested.

brief.protagonist: 12 Halsey, a 240-unit apartment building in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn
brief.stakes: The developers, EJS Group and Hope Street Capital, stand to gain a lower-cost, longer-term financing structure, while the lender, AllianceBernstein, takes on the risk of a floating-rate loan on a newly delivered property.
brief.tension: The refinancing replaces a $108.2 million construction loan with a $137.5 million loan, but the new loan is only for three years and floating-rate, leaving the sponsors exposed to interest rate swings and a near-term maturity.
brief.why_now: The deal is a fresh data point on how lenders are pricing newly delivered multifamily in Brooklyn, a market with heavy supply.
brief.lens_note: The refinancing shows capital moving from construction to stabilization, as the original construction loan is retired and new, more flexible debt is put in place.

brief.stakes: Brookfield is scaling up rapidly: record fundraising, a push into AI infrastructure, and full ownership of Oaktree. The stakes are its ability to deploy capital effectively and maintain investor confidence as it grows beyond $1 trillion in assets under management.
brief.tension: The tension is between scale and execution. Brookfield raised a record $77 billion, but deploying that capital wisely—especially in new areas like AI infrastructure—while integrating Oaktree and managing a much larger asset base is a challenge. The sources show no explicit constraint, but the implicit tension is whether the firm can sustain its growth without stumbling.
brief.why_now: The record fundraising and the Oaktree buyout signal a major consolidation in alternative asset management, with Brookfield positioning itself across credit, infrastructure, and AI. The quarter also shows how large managers are pivoting toward AI-related investments.
brief.number_that_matters: $77 billion raised in a single quarter. That's more than many sovereign wealth funds raise in a year, and it shows the scale of capital flowing into private markets and Brookfield's dominance.
brief.lens_note: Brookfield's record fundraising and deployment reflect a late-stage capital cycle where capital concentrates in the largest managers, and new frontiers like AI infrastructure attract massive commitments.

items.text: Brookfield Asset Management raised a company record $77 billion in the second quarter of 2026, bringing its assets under management to more than $1 trillion.
Year-to-date, the investor has brought in $98 billion, more than half of what Brookfield raised for all last year.
It also deployed $21 billion this past quarter.
Brookfield secured $5 billion in commitments for its first AI Infrastructure Fund.
Brookfield increased its financing framework with Bloom Energy for AI infrastructure power projects to $25 billion, up from the $5 billion commitment announced in October 2025.
Brookfield also completed its purchase of Oaktree, buying the remaining 26 percent stake for about $3 billion.
Brookfield’s seventh flagship private equity fund raised $6.7 billion during the quarter.
Its sixth flagship infrastructure fund brought in $9.3 billion.
Both are on pace to become the largest funds of their respective vintages.
On the real estate front, Brookfield raised $4.3 billion across segment funds and deployed $5.2 billion.
It bought a privately held U.S. manufactured-home portfolio and took an outdoor industrial storage portfolio private.
Net income grew to $1.17 billion this past quarter, almost double from a year prior.
Fee-related earnings climbed 20 percent year-over-year to $808 million.
Distributable earnings grew to $707 million, up by 15 percent year-over-year.
